title: The Moral Landscape
description: What ethics is, why it matters, and the major questions it asks

concepts.title: What Is Ethics?
concepts.contentHtml:
Ethics (or moral philosophy) is the systematic study of what makes actions right or wrong, what kinds of people we ought to be, and what makes lives go well.

It is divided into three main branches:

Normative ethics: theories about what is right — utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics.
Metaethics: questions about the nature of moral claims — are they true or false? Objective or subjective?
Applied ethics: using moral theory to address real problems — bioethics, business ethics, environmental ethics.

Ethics is not merely a matter of custom or law; a society can have unjust laws and a morally monstrous culture. Philosophy asks what we ought to do, not merely what we do.

concepts.title: Moral Realism and Anti-Realism
concepts.contentHtml:
Are moral claims objectively true or false, like facts about chemistry?

Moral realism: yes — moral facts exist independently of what anyone thinks. Plato's Forms included the Form of the Good. Contemporary realists like Derek Parfit and Russ Shafer-Landau defend it.

Expressivism (Ayer, Blackburn): moral statements express attitudes, not facts. 'Torture is wrong' means something like 'Boo torture!' — it doesn't describe the world.

Error theory (Mackie): moral statements aim to describe objective facts, but no such facts exist, so all positive moral claims are false.

This metaethical debate is foundational — it affects how seriously we should take ethical disagreement.

concepts.title: The Is–Ought Gap
concepts.contentHtml:
David Hume observed in the Treatise (1740) that moral arguments often slip from statements of fact ('is') to statements of obligation ('ought') without justification.

From 'humans evolved as social animals' we cannot automatically derive 'humans ought to be social.' The transition requires a bridge — a normative premise.

This is now called Hume's Law or the naturalistic fallacy (G.E. Moore's version): you cannot derive moral conclusions from purely natural facts without additional moral premises.

The is–ought gap motivates the search for distinctly normative foundations for ethics — whether in reason (Kant), consequences (utilitarians), or character (Aristotle).

title: Utilitarianism
description: The greatest happiness for the greatest number

concepts.title: Bentham's Calculus
concepts.contentHtml:
Jeremy Bentham founded classical utilitarianism: the right action is the one that maximises net pleasure over pain for all affected parties.

Bentham proposed a hedonic calculus to measure pleasure by intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent. Pleasure is pleasure — the only morally relevant difference is quantity.

'The question is not, can they reason? nor, can they talk? but, can they suffer?' Bentham famously extended moral concern to animals on this basis. Pain is bad wherever it occurs.

Bentham's utilitarianism is a purely consequentialist theory: the moral status of an action depends entirely on its outcomes.

concepts.title: Mill's Qualitative Utilitarianism
concepts.contentHtml:
John Stuart Mill modified Bentham by introducing quality of pleasure. Higher pleasures — intellectual, aesthetic, moral — are intrinsically more valuable than lower ones.

'It is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' The experienced judge who knows both kinds will prefer the higher, even at greater cost.

Mill also distinguished act utilitarianism (each act is judged by consequences) from the precursor to rule utilitarianism: follow the rules whose general adoption produces the most good. Rule utilitarianism handles objections about lying and promise-breaking more elegantly.

Mill argued utilitarianism is compatible with justice — rights protect utility in the long run.

concepts.title: Objections to Utilitarianism
concepts.contentHtml:
Utilitarianism faces powerful objections:

The utility monster (Nozick): a being that gets vastly more pleasure than others from resources should receive everything — a repugnant conclusion.

The transplant case: if a surgeon can save five dying patients by killing one healthy patient for organs, utilitarianism seems to demand it. Most find this monstrous.

Demandingness: if you must always maximise welfare, you should give all surplus income to effective charities — leaving nothing for personal projects.

Integrity (Bernard Williams): utilitarianism alienates you from your own projects and commitments by making everything hostage to the aggregate.

title: Deontological Ethics
description: Duty, rights, and the categorical imperative

concepts.title: Kant's Categorical Imperative
concepts.contentHtml:
Immanuel Kant argued that morality is grounded in reason, not consequences. The supreme moral principle is the Categorical Imperative — a command that holds unconditionally.

First formulation (universal law): 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' Lying fails because universal lying would destroy the institution of communication it exploits.

Second formulation (humanity): 'Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never as a means only.' Using people solely as tools violates their dignity as rational agents.

concepts.title: Rights-Based Deontology
concepts.contentHtml:
Rights-based deontologists hold that individuals possess moral rights that constrain what may be done to them, regardless of outcomes.

Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) argues that individuals have rights so strong that violating them is wrong even to produce better aggregate outcomes. 'Individuals are inviolable.'

W.D. Ross proposed prima facie duties: multiple duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence) each have genuine moral weight. When they conflict, we must use judgment — there is no single master principle. This pluralism is more realistic than Kant's single formula but less systematic.

concepts.title: Objections to Deontology
concepts.contentHtml:
Deontological ethics faces several serious challenges:

Absolutism: Kant held that lying is wrong even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding. Most find this implausible — rigid rules seem to forbid obvious goods.

Conflict of duties (Ross acknowledged): what happens when two duties clash? There is no deontological decision procedure for conflicts.

Threshold deontology: some rights-theorists allow consequentialist overrides when the stakes are catastrophically high — but then the view needs a principled account of the threshold.

Foundation problem: Kant claims the categorical imperative is derived from pure reason alone, but critics (Hegel, Korsgaard) question whether formal universalisability alone can generate rich moral content.

title: Virtue Ethics
description: Character, flourishing, and the good life

concepts.title: Aristotle's Eudaimonia
concepts.contentHtml:
Aristotle asked not 'what should I do?' but 'what kind of person should I be?' The goal of ethics is eudaimonia — often translated as flourishing, happiness, or the good life.

Eudaimonia is an activity, not a feeling: it is living well and doing well. It requires exercising distinctively human capacities — particularly reason — in accordance with virtue (arete).

Virtues are stable character traits — courage, justice, honesty, temperance — acquired through habituation. 'We become courageous by doing courageous things.' Character is the sediment of repeated action.

The virtuous person not only does the right thing but does it with the right motivation, at the right time, and with the right feeling — acting from an integrated self, not grudgingly.

concepts.title: The Doctrine of the Mean
concepts.contentHtml:
Aristotle located each virtue as a mean between two vices — a deficiency and an excess.

Courage is the mean between cowardice (deficiency) and recklessness (excess). Generosity is the mean between miserliness and prodigality. Proper pride is between servility and arrogance.

Crucially, the mean is not an arithmetic average — it is the right amount for the person and situation. What counts as courageous for a soldier differs from what counts as courageous for a physician. Practical wisdom (phronesis) is the meta-virtue of perceiving the mean correctly in concrete situations.

Modern revival: Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981) argued that the collapse of virtue ethics caused the incoherence of modern moral discourse.

concepts.title: Contemporary Virtue Ethics and Care Ethics
concepts.contentHtml:
Neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics has flourished since the mid-20th century:

Philippa Foot's Natural Goodness grounds virtues in what it is for a member of a species to function well — a naturalistic account avoiding the is–ought gap.

Rosalind Hursthouse applies virtue ethics to applied questions: abortion, vegetarianism, and the emotions, showing the framework's practical power.

Care ethics (Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings) extends virtue ethics: emphasising relationships, empathy, and responsiveness over universal principles. Moral life is not impartial — we have special obligations to those we are in relationships with. Critics worry care ethics privileges partiality in ways that could entrench injustice; defenders argue impartialism ignores what matters most to real human lives.

title: Applied Ethics and Hard Cases
description: Trolley problems, moral luck, and living with ethical uncertainty

concepts.title: Trolley Problems and Moral Intuitions
concepts.contentHtml:
Judith Jarvis Thomson's trolley problem (1985) and Philippa Foot's original (1967) have become the paradigm of applied moral thought-experiment.

A runaway trolley will kill five people. You can divert it to a side track where it kills one. Most say: divert — five lives outweigh one (utilitarian reasoning).

But the footbridge variant changes intuitions: you can stop the trolley by pushing a large man off a bridge to his death. Most say: don't push — even to save five.

The difference seems to involve using someone as a means vs. redirecting an existing threat. Deontologists exploit this distinction; utilitarians must explain why it matters. These cases isolate the doctrine of double effect and the act/omission distinction.

concepts.title: Moral Luck
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams independently identified moral luck: the uncomfortable fact that moral judgments are influenced by factors outside the agent's control.

Two equally negligent drivers: one reaches home safely; one hits a child who ran into the street. We judge the second driver more harshly — even though their negligence was identical. Our moral practices are sensitive to outcomes, not just intentions.

Types of moral luck: resultant (how outcomes fall), circumstantial (what situations you face), constitutive (who you are through upbringing and temperament), causal (if determinism is true).

Moral luck creates tension with the Kantian intuition that moral worth depends only on what is within your control.

concepts.title: Moral Uncertainty and Practical Wisdom
concepts.contentHtml:
We are often genuinely uncertain which moral theory is correct. How should we act under such moral uncertainty?

William MacAskill argues for maximising expected moral value: weight each theory's verdict by your credence in it. Others worry this treats moral theories like lotteries — misusing the notion of moral weight.

Strong intuitions can serve as data even when we can't systematise them. Rawls' method of reflective equilibrium: balance principles and intuitions, revising each to achieve coherence. Neither raw intuitions nor abstract theories have automatic veto.

The honest conclusion: ethics requires navigating genuine uncertainty with practical wisdom — theoretical knowledge, refined intuition, intellectual humility, and commitment to revision in light of better argument.
